Health and exercise are deeply connected aspects of human life that together form the foundation of a balanced active and disease-free lifestyle, and in today&apos;s modern world where sedentary habits stress and unhealthy eating are common their importance has increased more than ever before. Health does not only mean the absence of illness but a complete state of physical mental and social well-being, and regular exercise is one of the most effective ways to achieve and maintain this state. Exercise refers to any physical activity that improves or maintains physical fitness such as walking running yoga cycling swimming stretching or playing sports and even simple activities can produce powerful health benefits when practiced consistently. For example, a person who walks briskly for 30 minutes every day experiences better blood circulation improved heart function, and increased energy levels compared to someone who spends most of the day sitting. Regular exercise strengthens the cardiovascular system by making the heart more efficient at pumping blood which reduces the risk of heart diseases high blood pressure and stroke and this is why doctors often advise patients with heart-related issues to adopt light but regular physical activity. Exercise also plays a major role in maintaining a healthy weight as it helps burn excess calories and boosts metabolism; for instance a person who combines daily exercise with a balanced diet is more likely to maintain a healthy body weight than someone who relies only on dieting without physical activity. Apart from weight management exercise improves muscle strength bone density and joint flexibility, which is especially important as people age because strong muscles and bones reduce the risk of fractures arthritis and mobility problems; for example elderly individuals who practice light exercises like yoga or stretching often remain more independent and active in daily life.

Ancient India stands as one of the most remarkable and enduring civilizations in human history flourishing across thousands of years from the prehistoric era to the decline of the % Gupta Empire around 600 CE. Its origins trace back to early human settlements during the Stone Age when people lived in caves hunted animals and gradually learned to cultivate land and domesticate animals. The transition to the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods saw the rise of settled agricultural communities like MEHRGARH where early evidence of wheat cultivation and cattle rearing emerged. This slow yet steady progress in human organization and craftsmanship laid the foundation for the first great urban civilization of the subcontinent the Indus Valley Civilization: also known as the Harappan Civilization. The Indus Valley Civilization which thrived between 3300 BCE and 1500 BCE was one of the world&apos;s earliest examples of planned urban development. Its cities Harappa Mohenjo-Daro Lothal and Kalibangan featured well-laid streets advanced drainage systems public baths, granaries and standardized weights and measures. The people were skilled artisans who worked with metals beads and seals and they traded extensively with regions like Mesopotamia. Religious life seemed to revolve around the worship of nature and fertility symbols such as the Mother Goddess and Pashupati an early form of Lord Shiva. Although the script of this civilization remains UNDECIPHERED its art architecture and craftsmanship demonstrate a sophisticated society the civilization eventually declined possibly due to environmental changes, river shifts or invasions giving way to a new era in Indian history the Vedic Age. The Vedic period, spanning from around 1500 BCE to 600 BCE began with the arrival of Indo-Aryan tribes who settled along the rivers of Northwestern India

Giddha is one of the most vibrant, expressive, and culturally rich folk dances of Punjab representing the soul and spirit of Punjabi womanhood and capturing within its lively movements the essence of joy, freedom, laughter, strength and everyday life. This dance form performed exclusively by women has been a cherished part of Punjabi tradition for centuries passed down from generation to generation as an artistic expression that celebrates femininity community storytelling and cultural memory. When Punjabi women perform Giddha they do not merely dance they give voice to their emotions reveal their social experiences and express their inner vitality in a free and spirited manner. The core beauty of Giddha lies not only in the graceful movements but especially in the boliyan the short witty, rhythmic verses sung aloud by the performers. These boliyan act as windows into Punjabi village life capturing everyday stories teasing humor domestic relationships marital experiences social observations and even subtle critiques of societal norms. Through these verses women communicate their happiness, frustrations expectations wit and wisdom transforming Giddha into a platform for artistic expression and emotional release. Many of these boliyan are centuries old preserved in oral tradition while others are created spontaneously on the spot adding freshness and excitement to every performance. This improvisational nature of Giddha makes it a living evolving art form that adapts to time while retaining its traditional charm. Historically Giddha is believed to have emerged from ancient women&apos;s dances associated with seasonal festivities agrarian celebrations harvest rituals and community gatherings. Long before modern entertainment existed women in Punjabi villages would come together in courtyards fields and open spaces to sing dance and share life&apos;s experiences through Giddha

In earlier times zoos were mainly collections of animals owned by kings and rulers to show their power such as Mughal emperors keeping lions or exotic birds in royal gardens but today the concept of a zoo has completely changed and now focuses on animal welfare and environmental responsibility. A modern zoo tries to recreate natural habitats for animals for example instead of keeping a tiger in a small cage zoos now design large forest-like enclosures with trees water pools and hiding spaces so the tiger can behave naturally by walking resting and playing as it would in the wild. One of the most important roles of a zoo is wildlife conservation especially for endangered species whose numbers are rapidly decreasing due to deforestation climate change and illegal hunting; for instance animals like the giant panda white rhinoceros and certain species of deer have survived mainly because of breeding programs run by zoos across the world. These breeding programs are carefully planned to maintain genetic diversity and animals are sometimes exchanged between zoos in different countries such as giraffes being moved from one zoo to another to prevent inbreeding and ensure healthy offspring. Zoos also act as strong educational centers where students and visitors learn about animals their habitats and the importance of protecting nature and this learning becomes more effective because people can see real animals instead of only reading about them in books; for example when a child watches an elephant using its trunk to eat food or spray water the child understands animal behavior much better than through pictures alone.

Time management is not merely about creating a schedule or filling up a planner with long lists of tasks. It is a mindset, a method of approaching our day in a disciplined, intentional and thoughtful manner. Many people fail not because they lack talent or ambition, but because they spend their time reacting instead of planning, drifting instead of deciding and racing instead of focusing. To master time management, one must first acknowledge that time is a limited resource. Every minute wasted is gone forever, while every minute invested holds the power to create results, skills and progress. The most effective individuals prioritize tasks based on importance rather than urgency. Urgency tricks us into believing that immediate action equals meaningful achievement. Importance reminds us that long-term impact matters more than short bursts of activity. Successful students, professionals and entrepreneurs often begin their day by tackling their most meaningful task first, a technique known as &quot;eating the frog.&quot; It eliminates procrastination and builds momentum for the rest of the day. Another essential principle in time management is the power of routines. Morning and evening routines create structure, reduce decision fatigue and help maintain focus. When we automate small parts of our life, such as planning the next day before bed or reviewing our goals every morning, our brain is free to devote energy to creativity, learning and problem-solving. Equally important is learning to say no. Many people overload their schedules because they fear disappointing others. But every &quot;yes&quot; to a low-value activity is a &quot;no&quot; to something meaningful. Protecting your time means protecting your future. Breaks are not the enemy of productivity; they are fuel for the mind. Short intervals of rest enhance concentration, prevent burnout and boost creativity. Even the world&apos;s top performers follow cycles of work and rest.

A morning walk is usually taken early in the day, often at dawn, when the air is fresh, pollution is minimal, and the surroundings are calm and quiet, making it an ideal time for physical exercise and mental freshness; for example, a person who wakes up at 5:30 a.m. and goes for a walk in a nearby park experiences cool air, chirping birds, and rising sunlight, which naturally energizes the body and prepares the mind for the day ahead. Morning walks help regulate the biological clock of the body, improve digestion, boost metabolism, and enhance blood circulation, which is why doctors often recommend morning walks to people suffering from obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, or heart-related problems; for instance, a diabetic patient who walks briskly for 30 to 45 minutes every morning often notices better blood sugar control compared to someone who remains inactive. Morning walking also supports mental health, as exposure to early sunlight increases the production of serotonin, a hormone responsible for happiness and emotional stability, so people who regularly go for morning walks usually feel more positive, focused, and less stressed throughout the day. In addition to physical and mental benefits, a morning walk builds discipline and time management skills because waking up early and maintaining a routine requires consistency; for example, a student who develops the habit of morning walking often becomes more punctual and organized in studies and daily tasks. On the other hand, an evening walk is usually taken after completing the day&apos;s work, often around sunset or after dinner, and it serves as a relaxing activity that helps release the stress and fatigue accumulated during the day; for example, an office worker who spends long hours sitting in front of a computer may feel mentally exhausted, but a peaceful 20 to 30 minute evening walk helps relax muscles, refresh the mind, and improve mood.

Humanity&apos;s fascination with the Moon has evolved from poetic musings to rigorous scientific inquiry, revealing a satellite far more dynamic and complex than the lifeless orb we once imagined. Recent analyses of Apollo relics using modern techniques have shown that Space weathering driven by solar wind and micrometeoroid impacts produces Nanophase Iron particles on Lunar Soil grain rims, darkening ultraviolet reflectance in ways crucial for interpreting far-UV mapping data from instruments like the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter&apos;s LAMP, designed to detect water ice in shadowed craters. Seismic exploration has also reshaped our understanding: researchers scrutinizing imagery and Apollo-era sample sites found evidence that shallow Moonquakes attributed to tectonic activity along faults such as the Lee-Lincoln scarp have occurred in the Taurus-Littrow valley within the past 90 million years. These small-scale thrust faults indicate that tectonic contraction and orbital tidal forces remain active, prompting a Re-Evaluation of lunar interior dynamics and future landing site regulations. The presence of volatiles, particularly Water Ice in permanently shadowed polar craters, has galvanized efforts to design specialized instrumentation: NASA&apos;s Artemis program will deploy the Lunar Terrain Vehicle Equipped with AIRES and L MAPS sensors to map both surface minerals and subsurface ice to depths of over 40 meters. On the Surface, NASA&apos;s SLAP initiative will deploy DUSTER and SPSS payloads to characterize dust and plasma interactions near the lunar south pole, addressing challenges posed by abrasive regolith and charged dust that compromise habitats and spacesuits. These efforts are sparking urgent calls for updated International Legal Frameworks, as Countries like China plan crewed landings by 2030 and India&apos;s ambitious Chandrayaan 5/LUPEX mission coordinated with JAXA, NASA, and ESA prepares to probe Polar Volatiles with advanced Instrumentation.

Earthquakes along the ocean floor can cause tsunamis, giant tidal waves bringing immense destruction to coastal areas they hit. A similar phenomenon, called a seiche, can occur on lakes. Although! SEICHES are usually smaller than tsunamis, they are still capable of destroying lakefront property if the earthquake has sufficient force. Fires Earthquakes can also cause fires by pulling down power lines, ripping apart gas pipes, or toppling wood burning stoves or fireplaces. Although the resulting fires can vary in severity, their effect is often worsened as the earthquake disrupts emergency crew ability to extinguish them. The most obvious danger brought by earthquakes is shaking ground. Depending on its intensity, this motion itself can damage or destroy building materials, which get stretched and bent beyond their tolerances. The ground&apos;s movement can take the form of waves running along the surface of the ground. As the wave runs under a building, the structure can lean, potentially tipping over. Then, when the shaking stops, the ground often settles to a different level compared to where it was previously, causing buildings, roads, and other structures to become unstable, topple, or break apart. <LIQUEFACTION> is particularly common in places with sandy soil and groundwater at shallow depths in the soil. Displacement along Fault Lines When an area containing a fault line gets hit by an earthquake, the land can break into new masses, separated by the fault line. Structures that were built across the fault will then be cleaved apart. If a road, for example, happens to cross the fault line, it can be sliced apart at the fault, with the two new pieces separated by a chasm or even pushed past each other, depending on the movement of the earth&apos;s plates. As the soil firms, the building will stop settling and come to rest in its altered position.

Dimensions on the Importance of Transformational Leadership in Education Educational institutions need leaders that would confront the status quo and use their power to deal with power imbalances in schools and communities. An effective leader must be willing to use the authority of democracy if he is to achieve an institution improvement. Leadership is a crucial element concerned with creating conditions in which institutional reforms can succeed including improving students learning and institution&apos;s image. Effective leaders are found to exercise an indirect but powerful influence on the effectiveness of the institution and on the achievement of students. Traditionally, a principal&apos;s role performance involves focusing on institutional goals, the curriculum, instruction and creating conducive institutional environment. The principal focuses on enhancing teacher&apos;s performance and on the behaviours of teachers so as to enable teachers to engage their students in learning activities which ultimately focus on helping students learn. Thus, principal&apos;s leadership is thought to be instrumental in bringing about institutional effectiveness. This traditional approach to leadership is known as instructional leadership. The term instructional leadership emerged from institutional effectiveness research in the 1980s. However, instructional leadership suffers from some drawbacks. Dimmock (1995) asserts that instructional leadership is too prescriptive and relies on a top-down process of management. This type of structure supports the view that when principals accomplish vital tasks, teaching and learning improve. He suggests that institutions are characterized by loose coupling and autonomy and a better strategy would be a bottom-up approach.

Liberty is one of the most enduring and complex ideas in human thought, a concept that has animated revolutions, shaped constitutions, inspired art and literature, and guided the moral imagination of individuals across cultures and centuries, yet it remains elusive, contested, and perpetually unfinished in its realization; at its core, liberty refers to the condition in which individuals possess the capacity to think, choose, speak, and act without undue coercion, but this simple formulation conceals layers of philosophical, political, and social meaning that vary depending on historical context and human experience, for liberty is not merely the absence of chains or the removal of tyrants, but the presence of conditions that allow human potential to flourish with dignity and responsibility. From the earliest civilizations, people have struggled against domination, whether imposed by kings claiming divine authority, empires enforcing obedience through violence, or social hierarchies that confine individuals by birth, gender, caste, or race, and these struggles reveal that liberty is inseparable from power, because to be free is always to negotiate the limits of authority and the distribution of control within a society. Classical thinkers such as Aristotle distinguished between living as a slave and living as a citizen, suggesting that liberty required participation in public life, while later philosophers like John Locke framed liberty as a natural right inherent in the individual, grounded in reason and consent rather than tradition or force, a shift that profoundly influenced modern democratic thought. Yet even as liberty was proclaimed as universal, it was often denied in practice, most starkly in the coexistence of liberty rhetoric with slavery, colonialism, and exclusion, reminding us that liberty has historically

Drug addiction is a serious social, psychological, and health-related problem that affects individuals, families, and entire communities, and it refers to a condition in which a person becomes physically or mentally dependent on drugs or harmful substances, losing control over their use despite knowing the negative consequences. Drug Addiction often begins casually or experimentally, especially among teenagers and young adults, who may try substances out of curiosity, peer pressure, stress, or the desire to escape problems, but over time this occasional use can turn into a powerful dependency; for example, a student may start using drugs to cope with exam pressure or emotional pain, believing it will provide temporary relief, but gradually the body and mind become reliant on the substance, making it difficult to function without it. As Addiction deepens, individuals often experience physical problems such as weight loss, weakened immunity, liver damage, heart issues, and neurological disorders, while mental health issues like anxiety, depression, paranoia, and mood swings also become common; for instance, a drug-addicted person may appear restless, aggressive, or withdrawn and may struggle to Concentrate or make rational decisions. Dangerous aspect of drug addiction is tolerance and withdrawal, where the body requires increasing amounts of the drug to achieve the same effect, and stopping its use causes severe physical and psychological symptoms such as Nausea, Tremors, Sweating, Insomnia, and Intense Cravings, which often push the person back into addiction even after trying to quit. Drug addiction also increases the risk of life-threatening situations, including overdose, infectious diseases like HIV/AIDS and Hepatit is through shared needles, and Fatal Accidents due to impaired judgment and coordination;

Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is one of the most remarkable achievements in the history of India&apos;s Space program, known Worldwide for its reliability, versatility, and precision in delivering satellites into various orbits, especially the Sun-Synchronous-Orbit that is crucial for earth-observation missions. Developed by ISRO, PSLV transformed India from a nation dependent on Foreign Launch Services into a Global provider of Commercial Launches, Over the years, PSLV-C37 has carried out missions of Immense National &\@%! and International importance, such as placing the IRS and Cartosat Satellites that help India monitor agriculture, and urban planning, and its capabilities were proven on the world stage when it launched 104 satellites in a single flight during mission PSLV-C37, setting a record that showcased India&apos;s technological expertise. It also played a major role in Interplanetary exploration by successfully launching CHANDRAYAAN-1, India&apos;s first Lunar mission, and the Mars Orbiter Mission, which made India the first Country to reach Mars Orbit on its first attempt. Its variants such as PSLV-G, PSLV-CA, PSLV-XL and PSLV-DL provide flexibility for carrying different payloads, and this adaptability makes PSLV the preferred launcher for many International Customers seeking affordable, dependable access to space. Even with newer rockets like GSLV Mk-III and SSLV entering service, PSLV remains ISRO&apos;s workhorse because of its unmatched track record and continues to support India&apos;s growing role in global space missions, scientific research, commercial satellite deployment, and future exploratory projects that depend on accurate and cost-effective access to orbit.

Transformational leadership in education is often described as a process in which leaders work collaboratively with teachers, students and the wider community to build a shared sense of purpose. Rather than relying only on positional authority, transformational leaders seek to inspire others through vision, commitment, and mutual trust. In contemporary schooling environments, such leaders recognize that simply maintaining existing routines is insufficient when students needs and societal expectations continue to evolve. They therefore commit themselves to ongoing institutional learning, encouraging staff to reflect critically on current practices and to experiment with new approaches that may enhance student achievement. A transformational leader strives to develop the professional capacity of teachers by fostering collegiality, shared problem solving, and open communication. In this sense, leadership becomes a distributed activity rather than the responsibility of a single individual. When teachers feel supported and respected, they are generally more motivated to engage in innovative instruction and to respond constructively to student diversity. Importantly, transformational leadership is grounded in ethical considerations, including fairness, transparency and social justice. Educational institutions do not operate in isolation; they are influenced by community expectations, economic realities, and cultural norms. Leaders who understand these dynamics are better positioned to guide meaningful change. Although transformational leadership can be demanding, it provides a powerful framework for improving educational outcomes. By cultivating shared values, encouraging collaboration and modeling professional integrity, transformational leaders create learning environments that are inclusive, adaptive and forward-looking.

Most species burrow into the Soil and Bury Dung in tunnels directly UNDERNEATH the pats which are hollowed out from within. Some large species originating from France excavate tunnels to a depth of approximately 30 cm below the dung pat. These beetles make Sausage-Shaped brood chambers along the tunnels. The Shallowest tunnels belong to a much smaller Spanish species that buries dung in chambers that hang like fruit from the branches of a pear tree. South African beetles dig narrow tunnels of approximately 20 cm below the surface of the pat. Some Surface-Dwelling beetles including a South African species cut perfectly-shaped balls from the pat, which are rolled away and attached to the bases of plants. For maximum dung burial in Spring Summer and Autumn farmers require a variety of species with overlapping periods of activity. In the Cooler environments of the state of Victoria, the large French species (2.5 cms long) is matched with smaller (half this size) temperate-climate Spanish species. The former are slow to recover from the winter cold and produce only one or two generations of offspring from late spring until autumn. The latter which multiply rapidly in early spring, produce two to five generations annually. The South African ball-rolling species being a sub-tropical beetle, prefers the climate of northern and Coastal New South Wales where it commonly works with the South African tunneling species. In warmer climates many species are active for longer periods of the year.

Some years ago, when several theoretical physicists, principally Dirk Helbing and Boris Kerner of Stuttgart, Germany, began publishing papers on traffic flow in publications normally read by traffic engineers they were clearly working outside their usual sphere of Investigation. They had noticed that if they simulated the movement of Vehicles on a highway using the equations that describe how the molecules of a gas move some very Strange results emerged. Of course vehicles do not behave exactly like gas molecules: for example drivers try to avoid Collisions by slowing down when they get too near another Vehicle whereas gas molecules have no such concern the physicists modified the equations to take the differences into account and the overall description of traffic as a flowing gas has proved to be a very good one; the moving-gas model of traffic reproduces many phenomena seen in real-WORLD traffic. The Strangest thing that came out of these equations however was the implication that congestion can arise completely spontaneously no external causes are necessary. Vehicles can be flowing freely along at a density still well below what the road can handle and then suddenly gel into a slow-moving ooze. Under the right conditions a brief and local fluctuation in the speed or the distance between vehicles is all it takes to trigger a system-wide breakdown that persists for hours. In fact the physicists&apos; analysis suggested such Spontaneous breakdowns in traffic flow probably occur quite frequently on highways.

Though a decidedly unsettling discovery this showed Striking similarities to the phenomena popularized as &apos;chaos theory&apos;. This theory has arisen from the understanding that in any Complex interacting System which is made of many parts each part affects the others tiny Variations in one part of a Complex System can grow in huge but unpredictable ways. This type of dramatic change from one state to another is similar to what happens when a Chemical Substance changes from a Vapor to a liquid. It often happens that water in a Cloud remains as a gas even after its temperature and density have reached the point where it could Condense into water droplets. However if the vapor encounters a solid surface even something as small as a speck of dust Condensation can take place and the transition from vapor to liquid finally occurs. Helbing and Kerner see traffic as a complex interacting system. They found that a small fluctuation in traffic density can act as the &apos;speck of dust&apos; causing a sudden change from freely moving traffic to synchronized traffic when vehicles in all lanes abruptly slow down and start moving at the same speed making passing impossible. The physicists have Challenged proposals to set a maximum Capacity for Vehicles on highways. They argue that it may not be enough simply to limit the rate at which Vehicles are allowed to enter a highway, rather, it may be necessary to time each vehicle&apos;s entry onto a highway precisely to Coincide with a temporary drop in the density of vehicles along the road. The aim of doing this would be to smooth out any possible fluctuations in the road conditions that can trigger a change in traffic behavior and result in congestion.

The Science of Evolutionary relationships has undergone a major change in recent decades. It used to be the case that all the features of organisms were important in working out their family tree. But following the work of German Entomologist Willi Hennig many Evolutionary Scientists now believe that the only features which carry any useful information are the evolutionary &apos;novelties&apos; shared between organisms. Mice, lizards and fish for example all have backbones so the feature &apos;backbone&apos; tells us nothing about their evolutionary relationship. But the feature &apos;four legs&apos; is useful because it&apos;s an evolutionary novelty a characteristic shared only between the lizard and the mouse. This would suggest that the lizard and mouse are more closely related to each other than either is to the fish. This revolutionary approach is called CLADISTICS and it has been Central to the idea that birds evolved from Dinosaurs. The &apos;birds are dinosaurs&apos; theory was first developed by English palaeontologist Thomas Huxley (1825-1895). According to some accounts one evening Huxley went to dinner still thinking about a mystery dinosaur bone in his lab. He knew he was dealing with the lower leg bone of a meat-eating two-legged dinosaur belonging to the classification known as theropods but attached to the tibia was an unidentified extra bone. On the menu that evening was quail a small bird similar to a pheasant and Huxley noticed the same strange bone attached to the quail tibia on his plate. He later realised that it was in fact the bird&apos;s anklebone. More importantly Huxley concluded that its forms in both dinosaur and bird skeletons were so similar that they must be closely related.

Huxley&apos;s idea fell out of favour for fifty years following the 1916 publication of The Origin of Birds by the Danish doctor Gerhard Heilmann. During this time Heilmann&apos;s theory was widely accepted. Heilmann had noted that two-legged meat-eating Dinosaurs lacked Collarbones. In later evolutionary stages these bones fuse together to form the distinctive &apos;Y&apos;- shaped bone in a bird&apos;s neck known as the furcula. Heilmann proposed the notion that such a feature could not be lost and then re-evolve at a later date so dinosaurs could not be the ancestors of birds. Subsequent work has found up to 85 characteristics that tie dinosaurs and birds together. But what of Heilmann&apos;s missing bones? Visible light can stream through to maximise photosynthesis while infrared radiation is trapped in the space between the layers away from the plants. At the back of the greenhouse sits the third element the main Water-production unit. Just before entering this unit the humid air of the greenhouse mixes with the hot dry air from between the two layers of the roof. This means the air can absorb more moisture as it passes through a second perforated Cardboard wall. Finally the hot saturated air hits a condenser. This is kept cool by still more seawater. Drops of pure distilled water form on the condenser and flow into a tank for irrigating the crops. The greenhouse more or less runs itself. Sensors switch everything on when the sun rises and alter flows of air and seawater through the day in response to changes in temperature, humidity and sunlight. On windless days, a fan ensures a constant flow of air through the greenhouse. &apos;Once it is tuned to the local environment you don&apos;t need anyone there for it to work,&apos; says Paton. &apos;We can run the entire operation off one 13- amp plug and in future we could make it entirely independent of the grid powered from solar panels.

Quantum computing is emerging as one of the most significant technological developments of the 21st Century. Traditional Computers, which process information using bits represented as either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, commonly called Qubits. A Qubit can exist in multiple states through a principle known as superPOSITION. Another important concept, called Entanglement allows qubits to maintain relationships that can be used for complex calculations. These properties give quantum computers the potential to solve certain problems much faster than conventional machines. The future applications of quantum computing are expected to influence many industries. In medicine, Quantum Systems may help researchers analyse complicated Molecular structures and accelerate the discovery of new medicines. In finance, Quantum Algorithms could improve risk analysis portfolio optimisation and fraud detection. Scientists may use quantum computers to model Chemical reactions, advanced materials, climate systems and other processes that are extremely difficult to simulate using ordinary computers. Quantum technology will also create new challenges for Cybersecurity. Many current encryption systems depend on mathematical problems that are difficult for conventional computers to solve. Powerful quantum computers could potentially weaken some of these security methods. As a result, Governments, Universities and technology companies are developing post quantum (CRYPTO-GRAPHIC) techniques designed to protect sensitive information against future quantum attacks.

The Punjab and Haryana High Court is one of the important constitutional Courts of India. It is located in Chandigarh and serves as the common High Court for the states of Punjab and Haryana and the Union Territory of Chandigarh. The Court has a significant place in the Judicial system of Northern India. It deals with a wide range of matters involving Civil law, Criminal law, Constitutional questions, administrative decisions, service matters, property disputes, taxation, education and many other areas of law. The High Court functions under the Constitution of India and exercises powers granted to it by the Constitution and various laws enacted by Parliament and the State Legislatures. The history of the Court is closely connected with the development of the Judicial system in Punjab. Before Independence, Judicial institutions in the region operated under a different administrative and constitutional framework. After India became independent several changes were made to reorganize the Courts and administrative territories. The High Court of Judicature at Lahore was an important institution before partition. The partition of India in 1947, arrangements were made for the establishment of a new High Court for the Indian part of Punjab. The East Punjab High Court was established in 1947 and initially functioned from Shimla. Later, as the administrative structure of the region developed, the Court was shifted to Chandigarh. The famous High Court building in Chandigarh forms part of the Capitol Complex, which was designed by the renowned architect Le Corbusier. The building is recognized for its distinctive architectural character and is an important landmark of Chandigarh. With the reorganization of Punjab in 1966, the present judicial arrangement gradually took shape. Haryana was created as a separate state, while Chandigarh became a Union Territory. The High Court continued to serve Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh as a common institution. This arrangement makes the Punjab and Haryana High Court distinctive because one High Court exercises jurisdiction over two states and one Union Territory. The Punjab and Haryana High Court performs an important role in protecting the rights of citizens and maintaining the rule of law. A High Court is not merely a place where disputes are decided. It is also a constitutional institution responsible for ensuring that public authorities act according to law. Citizens may approach the High Court when they believe that their legal or constitutional rights have been violated. One of the important constitutional powers of a High Court is the power to issue writs. Under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, High Courts can issue appropriate writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for other legal purposes. These powers provide an important remedy to individuals against unlawful actions by government authorities and public institutions.

Writ jurisdiction is an important feature of the constitutional role of a High Court. This jurisdiction provides an important legal remedy in appropriate cases where a person challenges an unlawful action or seeks enforcement of a legal right. Different types of writs have different purposes. The writ of habeas corpus is generally associated with protection against unlawful detention. Mandamus may be issued in appropriate circumstances to require a public authority to perform a legal duty. Certiorari is generally concerned with the review of certain decisions of lower courts, tribunals or authorities. Prohibition may be used in appropriate circumstances to prevent a body from proceeding beyond its jurisdiction. Quo warranto concerns the legal authority of a person to hold a public office. A writ petition is a formal legal document. It may contain the facts of the case, grounds of challenge, legal arguments, supporting documents and the relief requested from the court. The preparation of such a petition requires careful attention because the court must be provided with relevant facts and legal grounds. Courts decide matters according to the Constitution, statutes, rules, precedents, evidence and the circumstances of each case. The availability of writ jurisdiction does not mean that every disagreement with a government decision automatically results in a writ being granted. The judicial system provides different legal remedies through which parties may challenge certain decisions. An appeal is a legal proceeding in which a higher court is asked to examine a decision of a lower court or authority, where an appeal is permitted by law. The scope and grounds of an appeal depend upon the nature of the case and the applicable statute. The Punjab and Haryana High Court hears various kinds of appeals within its jurisdiction. Civil and criminal matters may reach the High Court through appellate proceedings when the relevant law permits such an appeal. The court may examine questions of law, questions of fact, procedural issues or other matters depending upon the type of appeal. Review jurisdiction is governed by specific legal provisions and is generally exercised on limited grounds. A party cannot ordinarily use review proceedings simply to obtain a fresh hearing on every issue decided earlier.

A professional atmosphere helps courts focus on legal issues and contributes to the orderly administration of justice. The relationship between justice and technology is becoming increasingly important in the modern judicial system. Courts are responsible for protecting legal rights, resolving disputes, interpreting laws and ensuring that justice is delivered fairly. Technology can support these responsibilities by making judicial processes more organized, accessible, transparent and efficient. The Punjab and Haryana High Court, like other modern courts, operates in an environment where digital systems are becoming an important part of court administration and legal practice. One of the major developments in the judicial system is the use of electronic records and digital case management. Traditionally, courts depended heavily on physical files, registers and printed documents. Maintaining and searching through large numbers of physical records could require considerable time and effort. Digital systems can help store organize, search and retrieve information more efficiently. Properly maintained electronic records can also assist authorized users in obtaining case-related information without unnecessary delays. Online services have also changed the way lawyers and litigants interact with courts. Case status, cause lists orders, judgments and other information may be made available through official digital platforms. Electronic filing can reduce paperwork and make it possible to submit certain documents without requiring repeated physical visits to court offices. Such facilities can be especially useful for lawyers and litigants who are located far from the court. Technology can also support communication and virtual proceedings. Video conferencing facilities may allow hearings or meetings to take place when physical presence is difficult or unnecessary, subject to the applicable rules and directions of the court. This can save time and reduce travel requirements. However, virtual proceedings must maintain the same standards of fairness, discipline, confidentiality and legal procedure as physical proceedings. Artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies may also have a growing role in legal research and court administration. Computer systems can assist in searching large collections of legal documents organizing information, identifying relevant material and performing repetitive administrative tasks. These technologies can help legal professionals work more efficiently, but they should be treated as supporting tools rather than replacements for professional judgment. The use of technology in justice also creates important responsibilities. Digital systems must be protected against unauthorized access, data loss, manipulation and cyber threats. Personal and confidential information contained in legal documents requires careful handling. Courts and legal professionals must therefore follow appropriate security practices and ensure that technological development does not compromise privacy or fairness.

The effective functioning of such an institution requires not merely the availability of modern infrastructure, but also adherence to procedural discipline, judicial independence, professional ethics, institutional accountability and the principle that every dispute must ultimately be determined according to law. In an increasingly digitized environment, the administration of justice involves the systematic management of extensive quantities of information, including pleadings, affidavits, applications, documentary evidence, judicial precedents, statutory provisions and administrative correspondence. The transition from conventional paper-based records to electronically managed databases may substantially improve accessibility and efficiency; nevertheless, digitization simultaneously creates complex obligations relating to authentication, confidentiality, cybersecurity, data preservation, interoperability and controlled access. Technological modernization cannot be regarded merely as a mechanical substitution of computers for files; rather, it constitutes a comprehensive transformation of the manner in which judicial information is created, processed, communicated, preserved and retrieved. An important challenge before modern courts is the reconciliation of technological efficiency with procedural fairness. Automated systems may facilitate scheduling, indexing, document classification and information retrieval, but judicial determination necessarily involves contextual reasoning that cannot be reduced to numerical calculations or predetermined instructions. The interpretation of legislation may require consideration of constitutional principles, legislative intent, established precedent, factual circumstances and competing legal arguments. Technological instruments should assist judges and legal professionals without diminishing the independence, discretion and responsibility inherent in judicial decision-making. The increasing availability of electronic filing and virtual hearing facilities has also altered traditional patterns of legal practice. An advocate may now prepare and transmit documents electronically, examine case information remotely and participate in proceedings through approved digital mechanisms. Judicial review envisages not only a mere right of the citizen to raise the challenge before the Court and the mere power of the Court to take up the petition of such citizen for adjudication; but also the power with the Court to pronounce upon the result of such adjudication by deciding upon the action under challenge as void or illegal or rendering such action or the effect thereof as non-existent. The impairment of any one of these elements is bound to exclude the judicial review. On a particular aspect the power to pronounce upon the result of such adjudication can be unrestricted in terms of subject matter and the criteria test to be applied for coming to the conclusion as to the result of such adjudication or such power could be restricted in terms of such subject matter or in terms of the criteria to be applied. Originally the Constitution contained only a few subject matters qua which the judicial review on the alter of fundamental rights was excluded. However, the 1st amendment of Constitution had inflicted blow upon power of the judicial review on both the above said counts. By inserting Article 31-B, it had taken away from judicial review the subject matter included in the Ninth Schedule, as well as the criteriatest to be applied for judicial review of such subject matter i.e. violation of fundamental rights. The judgment rendered in Sankari Prasad's case (supra) upheld the double blow caused by the 1st amendment . It upheld the exclusion of the subject mater on the ground that such exclusion does not impinge upon the power of judicial review conferred upon Constitutional Courts, rather it only withdraws some subject matter from the scope of the judicial review. If one is to keep the linguistics and the logic intact then it is hard to resist a conclusion to the contrary, however, since the finding had come from the Supreme Court, therefore, it is to be accepted as it is. Article 31-B was upheld on the premise that it was not ordinary law and thus, not hit by Article 13. In addition, Article 32 of the Constitution gives an extensive original jurisdiction to the Supreme Court in regard to enforcement of Fundamental Rights. It is empowered to issue directions orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari to enforce them. The Supreme Court has been conferred with power to direct transfer of any civil or criminal case from one State High Court to another State High Court or from a Court subordinate to another State High Court. The Supreme Court, if satisfied that cases involving the same or substantially the same questions of law are pending before it and one or more High Courts or before two or more High Courts and that such questions are substantial questions of general importance, may withdraw a case or cases pending before the High Court or High Courts and dispose of all such cases itself. Under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, International Commercial Arbitration can also be initiated in the Supreme Court. The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court can be invoked by a certificate granted by the High Court concerned of the Constitution in respect of any judgement, decree or final order of a High Court in both civil and criminal cases, involving substantial questions of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution. Appeals also lie to the Supreme Court in civil matters if the High Court concerned certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance and that in the opinion of the High Court. The said question needs to be decided by the Supreme Court. In criminal cases, an appeal lies to the Supreme Court if the High Court has on appeal reversed an order of acquittal of an accused person and sentenced him to death or to imprisonment for life or for a period of not less than 10 years or has withdrawn for trial before itself any case from any Court subordinate to its authority and has in such trial convicted the accused and sentenced him to death or to imprisonment for life or for a period of not less than 10 years or certified that the case is a fit one for appeal to the Supreme Court. Parliament is authorised to confer on the Supreme Court any further powers to entertain and hear appeals from any judgement, final order or sentence in a criminal proceeding of a High Court. 	The Supreme Court has also a very wide appellate jurisdiction over all Courts and Tribunals in India in as much as it may, in its discretion, grant special leave to appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution from any judgment. The Supreme Court has special advisory jurisdiction in matters which may specifically be referred to it by the President of India under Article 143 of the Constitution. Under Order XL of the Supreme Court Rules the Supreme Court may review its judgment. Order but no application for review is to be entertained in a civil proceeding except on the grounds mentioned in Order XLVII, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in a criminal proceeding except on the ground of an error apparent on the face of the record.

That it is not a unitary and centralised Government or India but a division of powers and functions and only such central control as the Constitution has provided. The States their legislative executive and judicial functions are not mere administrative convenience of the Union to be set aside and overcome at every convenient turn. They represent a carefully balanced and constitutionally decentralised and integrated distribution of powers among different constitutionally recognised both is who must act within their respective spheres marked out by elaborate scheme of carefully chosen legislative entries in the 7th Schedule of the Constitution. It cannot be too strongly emphasised that under the Constitution, administration of justice is not a Union but a State subject for legislation and it will be an infraction of this Constitution to control such administration of justice by the backdoor of Constitution and Organisation which alone is the Union Legislative competence. A healthy routine improves concentration, energy and decision-MAKING. Every new day provides another opportunity to improve ourselves. We may not be able to change our past mistakes, but we can learn from them and make better decisions in the present. We may not control every situation, but we can control our attitude, effort and response.

EXERCISE 1: Access to Justice
### English @PSSSB
---
The Constitution of India guarantees to every citizen the right to approach a court of law for the redress of a grievance. However, the right to justice has little meaning if a person cannot afford the services of a lawyer or the expenses of litigation. For this reason, the State has a duty to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities. Legal services authorities have been set up at the national, state and district levels to give free legal aid to the weaker sections of society. Persons belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, women, children, victims of trafficking, industrial workmen, and persons in custody are entitled to such help. Lok Adalats are organised at regular intervals so that pending disputes may be settled amicably, without the delay and expense of a formal trial. A settlement reached in a Lok Adalat is treated as a decree of a civil court and is final and binding on all the parties. No appeal lies against such an award. Court fee paid in the matter is refunded in full. These measures reduce the burden on courts and give people a quick and affordable way to end their disputes. It is the duty of every officer of the court to make litigants aware of these facilities. A justice system that is easy to reach, quick to act and fair in its decisions is the surest foundation of a peaceful society. Awareness is the first step towards access. Many persons in villages and small towns do not know that free legal aid is available to them, or that a legal services clinic exists in their own area. Para-legal volunteers, panel lawyers and legal literacy camps have therefore been arranged so that the message may reach the last person in the queue. Posters, public announcements and help desks at court complexes also serve this purpose. A person who applies for legal aid is not required to pay any fee to the lawyer appointed for him. The authority also bears the cost of copies of documents and of other charges connected with the case. The lawyer is expected to take as much care of the case as he would take of the matter of a paying client. In this way, the poor man stands on an equal footing with the rich before the law, and the promise of equal justice becomes a reality.

EXERCISE 2: Computerisation of Courts
### English @PSSSB
---
In recent years, the use of technology in the judicial system has grown steadily. Case information that was once found only in thick registers kept in the record room can now be seen on a computer screen within a few seconds. Lawyers and litigants can check the status of a case, the date of the next hearing and the text of an order from their own homes without visiting the court. The e-filing system allows petitions, applications and documents to be submitted online. This saves time, reduces the use of paper and lowers the cost of travel for advocates who live far from the court. Digital signatures are used to confirm the identity of the person who submits a document. Fees may also be paid through the internet. Video conferencing facilities have made it possible to record evidence and to hear parties who are unable to attend in person. During the period of the pandemic, courts across the country relied heavily on virtual hearings so that urgent matters could continue to be heard. Many of these practices have now become a regular part of court work. Staff members must therefore learn to work quickly and accurately on a computer. Speed in typing, care in checking the typed matter, and respect for the confidentiality of court records are all essential qualities for those who serve in the courts of today. However, the move towards digital working has its own difficulties. In some areas the internet connection is weak, and many litigants are not familiar with computers or mobile applications. For this reason, help centres have been opened in court complexes where trained staff assist the public in filing cases and in finding case information. Training programmes are also held from time to time for officers and employees so that they may learn the use of new software. Safety of data is another matter of great importance. Passwords must be kept secret and must be changed at regular intervals. A computer should never be left open when the user goes away from the seat. Copies of important files should be saved in a safe place so that they are not lost if a machine fails. If the employees remain careful and alert, the courts will be able to enjoy all the benefits of technology without risk to the records of the people.

EXERCISE 3: Duties of a Court Employee
### English @PSSSB
---
A person who serves in a court holds a position of trust. The public looks to the court as the last hope for justice, and the conduct of every employee, whether high or low in rank, affects the faith that people place in the institution. An employee must therefore be honest, polite and punctual at all times. Official records must be kept safe and in proper order. No file, paper or document may be shown to an outsider, and no information about a pending case may be given to any person who is not entitled to receive it. Any attempt to influence the result of a case through an employee is a serious matter and must be reported to the senior officer at once. An employee should attend the office at the prescribed time and should not leave the seat during working hours without permission. Work received during the day should be disposed of on the same day, as far as possible. Where a delay is unavoidable, the reason should be noted on the file so that the responsible officer may take a decision. Courtesy towards advocates, litigants and fellow employees is expected. A patient hearing and a clear reply cost nothing, but they leave a lasting impression. A disciplined, hardworking and honest staff is the real strength of any court, and it is through such service that the dignity of the judiciary is preserved. Every employee is also expected to maintain a neat and clean office. Files should be arranged in the proper order, old records should be sent to the record room at the right time, and the desk should be kept free from needless papers. A well kept office saves much time, because any paper that is needed can be traced at once without a long search. This habit shows the care and the love of order that a good employee has. An employee must also be ready to learn. Rules and procedures are changed from time to time, and new circulars are issued by the High Court and by the government. It is the duty of each person to read them carefully and to act according to them. Where a doubt arises, he should ask his senior officer instead of guessing the answer. Honest work, regular study and a helpful manner will help an employee to grow in service and to win the respect of all.

EXERCISE 4: Right to Information
### English @PSSSB
---
The Right to Information Act was passed so that citizens may know how public authorities work and how public money is spent. Transparency in government makes officers more careful in the performance of their duties and helps to check corruption. A person who wants information may make a written request to the Public Information Officer of the department concerned, along with the prescribed fee. The officer is required to supply the information within thirty days of receiving the request. Where the matter concerns the life or liberty of a person, the reply must be given within forty-eight hours. If the request is refused, or if the applicant is not satisfied with the reply, he may file a first appeal before the senior officer of the same department, and thereafter a second appeal before the Information Commission. The Act also protects certain kinds of information from disclosure. Matters that affect the security of the country, the privacy of an individual, or the progress of an investigation need not be made public. The law therefore tries to keep a fair balance between the right of the citizen to know and the need of the State to keep certain secrets. Every public office must display the names of its information officers and must arrange its records in a way that makes them easy to search. When the citizen asks and the office answers, the bond of trust between the people and the administration becomes stronger. The Act has brought about a great change in the working of public offices. Records that were earlier kept hidden are now opened to inspection, and officers know that their decisions may be questioned by any citizen. Many irregularities in the distribution of ration, pensions and scholarships have come to light only through applications filed under this law. The Act has thus become a strong weapon in the hands of ordinary people. At the same time, the right must be used with responsibility. Applications should be clear and should ask for specific information, and they should not be filed merely to trouble an officer. The Public Information Officer, on his part, must reply in a polite manner and within the time allowed by law. A penalty may be imposed on an officer who refuses to give information without a good reason or who gives false or incomplete replies. A right that is used wisely benefits the whole society.

EXERCISE 5: Protection of the Environment
### English @PSSSB
---
The environment is the common inheritance of all living beings, and its protection is the duty of every citizen. The Constitution directs the State to protect and improve the natural surroundings and to safeguard forests and wildlife. It also lays down that it is the duty of each person to have compassion for living creatures. In many cities, the quality of the air has fallen sharply because of smoke from vehicles, factories and the burning of crop residue. Rivers have become polluted by sewage and industrial waste, and groundwater is being drawn out faster than it is replaced. If this goes on, future generations will find it hard to get clean water to drink and fresh air to breathe. Courts have played an important part in this field. Through their decisions, they have ordered the closure of polluting units, the planting of trees, and the proper treatment of waste. The principle that the polluter must pay the cost of cleaning up the damage has been accepted and applied in many cases. But laws and orders alone cannot achieve much. Each person can help by saving water and electricity, avoiding the use of plastic bags, planting saplings, and travelling together in shared vehicles. Small steps taken by many people can bring great and lasting changes to the land on which we live. Trees are among our best friends. They give shade and fruit, they hold the soil in place, they take in harmful gases and they give out the oxygen that we need to live. A single full-grown tree may serve a whole neighbourhood for many years. Yet forests are being cut down to make room for roads, buildings and farms, and the loss of green cover has led to floods in some places and to droughts in others. The use of clean energy is another step in the right direction. Sunlight and wind can be used to produce electricity without smoke or harmful waste, and many homes and offices have already begun to install solar panels. Waste should be sorted at the source into dry and wet portions so that it may be recycled or turned into manure. Schools should teach children from an early age to love nature, because a habit formed in childhood is seldom lost in later years.

EXERCISE 6: Procedure for Filing a Civil Suit
### English @PSSSB
---
A civil suit begins with the presentation of a plaint before the court that has the power to hear the matter. The plaint must contain the name of the court, the names and addresses of the parties, the facts that give rise to the claim, the relief that is asked for, and the value of the subject matter for the purpose of court fee and jurisdiction. It must be signed and verified by the plaintiff. After the plaint is accepted, the court issues a summons to the defendant, directing him to appear on a fixed date and to file a written statement within thirty days. If he fails to do so without good reason, the court may proceed against him in his absence and may pass an order in favour of the plaintiff.On the next stage, the court frames the issues that arise between the parties. Both sides then produce their documents and list their witnesses. Evidence is recorded, and each witness may be cross-examined by the opposite party. After this, the advocates present their final arguments.

When the arguments are over, the court pronounces its judgment in open court. A decree is then drawn up in accordance with the judgment. The party who is not satisfied with the result may file an appeal before the higher court within the time allowed by law, along with a certified copy of the decree.

Before filing a suit, a person should consider whether the matter can be settled without going to court. In certain cases, a notice must first be served upon the other side, giving a reasonable time to put right the wrong that has been done. Many disputes end at this stage through talks between the parties or through the help of a mediator. A suit should be filed only when all other efforts have failed.

The law also fixes a time limit within which a suit must be brought. If the period of limitation expires, the claim may be barred, even though the plaintiff has a good case on the merits. Interim orders, such as a temporary injunction or the appointment of a receiver, may be asked for by a separate application when the property or the rights of a party are in danger of being lost. Throughout the case, the parties must obey the directions of the court and must attend on the dates fixed.

EXERCISE 7: The Importance of Punctuality

### English @PSSSB
---
Time is the one resource that cannot be bought, stored or recovered once it is lost. A person who values time is respected by others, because he shows that he values their time as well. In an office, even a small delay by one person can hold up the work of several others and can cause great inconvenience to the public.

Punctuality is not merely a matter of reaching the workplace at the right hour. It also means finishing a task within the period given for it, replying to letters without delay, and keeping every appointment. Habits of this kind are formed in youth and remain with a person throughout life.

Many successful persons have said that their achievements owe a great deal to the careful use of each day. They made a plan in the morning, set aside the most important work for the best part of the day, and did not leave for tomorrow what could be done today. Such discipline is available to everyone, whatever his position.

In government service, delay in the disposal of files is often described as a form of denial of justice to the citizen who is waiting for a decision. An employee who is regular and prompt does a real service to the people. Good habits learnt today will serve a person well in every field of life.

A student who reaches school ahead of time finds his mind calm and ready to learn, while the one who arrives late is hurried and anxious for the whole day. The same is true of a clerk who comes to office a few minutes early. He can arrange his table, read the instructions of his officer and plan the work of the day without any rush. Such small habits make a large difference over the years.

Delay often begins with small excuses, such as waking late, waiting for a friend, or putting off a letter that can be written in five minutes. If these excuses are allowed to grow, they become a habit that is hard to break. A simple remedy is to keep a diary, to note down every task along with the date by which it must be done, and to check the list at the end of each day. A person who follows this method seldom misses a date.

EXERCISE 8: Safety in Cyberspace

### English @PSSSB
---
The internet has become a part of daily life. People use it to send messages, make payments, buy goods and gather information. However, this convenience carries risks, and those who do not take care may lose their money or their personal details to criminals who work online.

One common trick is to send a message that appears to come from a bank, asking the receiver to share a password, a card number or a one-time code. No genuine bank asks for such details by telephone or by message. A person who receives such a request should not reply and should report it to the bank and to the cyber crime police at once.

Strong passwords are the first line of defence. A good password is long, mixes letters, numbers and symbols, and is not used on more than one account. Software on computers and mobile phones should be updated regularly, because updates close gaps that criminals use to enter a system. Public wireless networks should not be used for banking.

Parents and teachers should also guide young people on the safe use of social media. Photographs and private information once posted may be copied and misused. A little caution before clicking on an unknown link or opening an unexpected attachment can save a great deal of trouble later on.

Online shopping and digital payments are useful, but they need care. Before making a payment, one should check that the website address is correct and that the page is secure. Offers that promise very large gifts or prizes in return for a small fee are almost always a fraud. Likewise, a stranger who calls to say that a parcel is held up, or that an account will be closed, should be treated with suspicion and the call should be ended at once.

If a person becomes a victim of online fraud, he should act without delay. The bank should be asked to block the card or the account immediately, and a complaint should be made on the national cyber crime helpline or on its official website. The sooner the matter is reported, the better the chance of stopping the transfer of money. Keeping screen shots of messages and records of the transaction will help the police in their inquiry. Awareness and quick action are the best protection.

EXERCISE 9: Public Health and Hygiene

### English @PSSSB
---
Good health is the greatest wealth a person can have, and the health of the community depends on the habits of each individual. Clean drinking water, proper disposal of waste, and clean surroundings prevent many diseases that otherwise spread quickly, especially in crowded towns and villages.

Washing the hands with soap before meals and after using the toilet is a simple practice that can prevent many infections. Food should be kept covered, and fruits and vegetables should be washed before they are eaten. Water that is not known to be safe should be boiled or filtered before use. Stagnant water around the house should be removed, as it provides a place where mosquitoes breed.

Government hospitals and health centres offer vaccines to children and expectant mothers free of charge. Parents should make sure that every child receives all the doses on time. Regular check-ups also help to find illnesses like diabetes and high blood pressure at an early stage, when they are easier to control.

Exercise and a balanced diet are equally important. A walk of thirty minutes every day, enough sleep, and a reduced intake of sugar and oil help a person to remain active and cheerful. A healthy people make a strong nation, and each of us must do our part to keep our community free from disease.

Mental health is as important as bodily health. Worry, fear and loneliness, if they are not dealt with in time, may lead to sleeplessness and to serious illness. A person who feels troubled should speak to a family member, a friend or a doctor instead of keeping the burden alone. Time spent with the family, a hobby, prayer or meditation, and a little rest from the mobile phone can bring peace to the mind and strength to the body.

Bad habits like smoking, chewing tobacco and the use of drugs ruin the health of the person and bring suffering to the family. Young people should keep away from them and should find healthy ways of enjoying themselves, such as games, music and reading. Employers and officers can also help by arranging health camps, by allowing time for rest, and by keeping the place of work clean and well lit. When health is looked after in this manner, the whole community enjoys a better and longer life.

EXERCISE 10: Importance of Education

### English @PSSSB
---
Education is the key that opens the door to progress, both for the individual and for the nation. It teaches a person to think clearly, to judge between right and wrong, and to earn an honest living. A country whose people are educated can make better use of its resources and can resist the spread of superstition and injustice.

The Constitution makes it the duty of the State to provide free and compulsory education to all children between the ages of six and fourteen years. Many schemes have been started to bring children to school, such as free textbooks, scholarships and midday meals. Special attention is given to girls and to children from poor families so that no child is left behind.

However, getting a child into a school is only the first step. The quality of teaching, the condition of school buildings and the availability of trained teachers are equally important. Parents also have a role to play by taking an interest in the studies of their children and by meeting teachers from time to time.

Education does not end with a degree. In a world that changes quickly, a person must keep learning new skills throughout life. Teachers hold a very important place in the field of education. For this reason, the selection, training and welfare of teachers must receive the highest attention of the State. Respect shown to the teacher by the pupil and by the community also adds greatly to the dignity of the profession.

Modern technology has opened new doors for learners. Lessons may now be seen on a screen, books may be read on a phone, and a student in a remote village can listen to an expert who lives in a distant city. EXERCISE 11: Office Correspondence and Official Language

### English @PSSSB
---
Letters and notes written in a government office should be short, clear and correct. The reader should be able to understand the purpose of the letter at the first reading. Long sentences, difficult words and needless repetition should be avoided, since they waste the time of the reader and may cause misunderstanding.

Every official letter should bear a reference number and the date, and should be addressed to the proper officer by designation. The subject should be stated in a single line, and the body should deal with one matter at a time. If a reply is awaited by a particular date, this should be stated plainly. The letter closes with a courteous phrase, followed by the signature and designation of the sender.

While typing a letter, the clerk must check the spelling of names, the figures of dates and amounts, and the correctness of the address. A mistake in a single figure may change the meaning of an order and may cause loss to a party. The typed copy should be read once again, line by line, against the draft before it is placed before the officer for signature.

Copies should be sent to all the offices concerned, and a file copy must be kept in the record. Good correspondence reflects the efficiency of the office. Neat typing, correct language and prompt despatch together create a favourable impression of the institution in the minds of the public.

The language used in an official letter must be polite but firm. Words such as 'kindly' and 'it is requested' are used when a favour is asked, while the words 'it is directed' are used when an order is passed. Abbreviations should be avoided unless they are well known, and the names of persons and offices should be written in full when they are used for the first time. A letter that is courteous in tone seldom fails to receive a prompt reply.

Replies to letters should be sent within the time fixed by the rules, and a reminder should be issued when the answer is delayed. Urgent matters should be marked as such on the cover, and the word 'Immediate' should not be used for ordinary letters, as this reduces its value. Letters of a confidential nature must be placed in a sealed cover and handed over only to the person to whom they are addressed. Care in these small matters is a mark of a well run office.

उठता, पढ़ाई करता, घर के कामों में माता-पिता की सहायता करता और फिर अपने लक्ष्य के लिए मेहनत करता। शुरुआत में उसे कई कठिनाइयों का सामना करना पड़ा। कभी पढ़ाई में मन नहीं लगता था, कभी थकान महसूस होती थी और कभी उसे लगता था कि उसके प्रयास व्यर्थ जा रहे है। फिर भी उसने हार नहीं मानी। समय बीतता गया। धीरे-धीरे उसकी आदतें बदलने लगीं। वह पहले से अधिक अनुशासित और आत्मविश्वासी हो गया। उसके शिक्षक भी उसकी लगन से प्रभावित हुए और उसे आगे बढ़ने के लिए प्रोत्साहित करने लगे। कुछ वर्षों बाद अर्जुन ने एक महत्वपूर्ण परीक्षा उत्तीर्ण कर ली। यह सफलता उसके लिए केवल एक उपलब्धि नहीं थी, बल्कि उसकी निरंतर मेहनत का प्रमाण थी। जब वह अपने गाँव लौटा तो लोगों ने उसका स्वागत किया। सभी जानना चाहते थे कि उसने इतनी बड़ी सफलता कैसे प्राप्त की। अर्जुन ने मुस्कुराते हुए कहा कि सफलता का कोई छोटा रास्ता नहीं होता। यदि व्यक्ति अपने लक्ष्य को स्पष्ट रखे, नियमित अभ्यास करे और कठिन समय में भी धैर्य बनाए रखे, तो सफलता अवश्य मिलती है। उसकी बातों ने गाँव के युवाओं को प्रेरित किया। उन्होंने भी अपने जीवन में अनुशासन और परिश्रम को महत्व देना शुरू किया। अर्जुन की कहानी पूरे क्षेत्र में प्रसिद्ध हो गई। लोग उसे केवल उसकी सफलता के लिए नहीं, बल्कि उसके संघर्ष, धैर्य और सकारात्मक सोच के लिए याद करने लगे। इस प्रकार एक साधारण गाँव का लड़का अपने कर्मों और दृढ़ निश्चय के बल पर अनेक लोगों के लिए प्रेरणा का स्रोत बन गया।

### Hindi Paragraph Special 2
---
समय मनुष्य के जीवन की सबसे मूल्यवान संपत्ति है। यह एक ऐसा संसाधन है जिसे न तो संग्रहित किया जा सकता है और न ही एक बार बीत जाने के बाद वापस प्राप्त किया जा सकता है। संसार में प्रत्येक व्यक्ति को प्रतिदिन समान चौबीस घंटे प्राप्त होते है, लेकिन उनकी सफलता और उपलब्धियाँ इस बात पर निर्भर करती है कि वे अपने समय का उपयोग किस प्रकार करते है। जो व्यक्ति समय का सम्मान करता है, समय भी उसका साथ देता है। वहीं जो लोग समय को व्यर्थ कार्यों में नष्ट कर देते है, उन्हें बाद में पछताना पड़ता है। समय का महत्व जीवन के प्रत्येक क्षेत्र में देखा जा सकता है। एक विद्यार्थी यदि नियमित रूप से अपने अध्ययन के लिए समय निर्धारित करता है, तो वह परीक्षा में अच्छे परिणाम प्राप्त कर सकता है। इसी प्रकार एक व्यापारी यदि अपने कार्यों को समय पर पूरा करता है, तो उसका व्यवसाय तेजी से आगे बढ़ सकता है। समय का सही प्रबंधन व्यक्ति को अनुशासित, संगठित और आत्मविश्वासी बनाता है। इसके विपरीत समय की उपेक्षा करने से अव्यवस्था, तनाव और असफलता का सामना करना पड़ सकता है। प्रकृति भी हमें समय का महत्व सिखाती है। सूर्य प्रतिदिन निश्चित समय पर उदय और अस्त होता है। ऋतुएँ अपने निर्धारित समय पर आती और जाती है। यदि प्रकृति का यह क्रम बाधित हो जाए, तो जीवन का संतुलन बिगड़ सकता है। इसी प्रकार मनुष्य के जीवन में भी समयबद्धता आवश्यक है। आज के आधुनिक युग में लोगों के पास अनेक सुविधाएँ उपलब्ध है, फिर भी समय की कमी की शिकायत अक्सर सुनने को मिलती है। इसका मुख्य कारण समय का अनुचित उपयोग है। कई लोग अपना बहुमूल्य समय बिना किसी उद्देश्य के मोबाइल फोन, सामाजिक माध्यमों या अन्य अनावश्यक गतिविधियों में व्यतीत कर देते है। यदि वही समय किसी उपयोगी कार्य, अध्ययन, कौशल विकास या स्वास्थ्य सुधार में लगाया जाए, तो जीवन में सकारात्मक परिवर्तन लाया जा सकता है। समय प्रबंधन की आदत बचपन से विकसित की जानी चाहिए। कार्यों की प्राथमिकता तय करना, दैनिक कार्यक्रम बनाना और निर्धारित समय सीमा में कार्य पूरा करना अत्यंत लाभदायक होता है। इससे व्यक्ति की कार्यक्षमता बढ़ती है और वह अपने लक्ष्यों की ओर अधिक प्रभावी ढंग से आगे बढ़ सकता है। सफल व्यक्तियों के जीवन का अध्ययन करने पर यह स्पष्ट होता है कि उन्होंने अपने समय का सदुपयोग किया और प्रत्येक क्षण को मूल्यवान समझा। कहा जा सकता है कि समय जीवन का आधार है। धन, पद और प्रतिष्ठा पुनः प्राप्त किए जा सकते है, लेकिन खोया हुआ समय कभी वापस नहीं आता। इसलिए प्रत्येक व्यक्ति को समय का सम्मान करना चाहिए और उसका उपयोग सोच-समझकर करना चाहिए। जो व्यक्ति समय का सही उपयोग करना सीख लेता है, वह जीवन में सफलता, संतोष और प्रगति के नए आयाम स्थापित कर सकता है।
